representativeRepos.readmeText:
security-audit

 A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

 This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness . The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

 What it does

 The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

- Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json .

- Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.

- Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.

- Structured output -- write confirmed , needs_validation , and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json .

- Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.

- Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md , FINDINGS-DETAIL.md , and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

 The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

 The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

 Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

 Files

 File
 Purpose

 SKILL.md
 Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns

 RECONNAISSANCE.md
 Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions

 HUNTING.md
 Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules

 ATTACK-CLASSES.md
 Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts

 MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md
 Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets

 AI-AND-LLM.md
 Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets

 WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md
 HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets

 CLIENT-SIDE.md
 DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets

 SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md
 Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes

 CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md
 IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes

 PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md
 RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes

 RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md
 Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes

 DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md
 Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes

 DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md
 Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes

 VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md
 Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting

 report-schema.json
 JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts

 validate-findings.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5

 validate-findings.test.cjs
 Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks

 validate-coverage-ledger.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5

 validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs
 Coverage-ledger validator tests

 Installation

 Install the skill with the Skills CLI :

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit

 Use --global for a user-level installation:

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit \
 --global

 Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

 Usage

 Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

 security audit this codebase

 find security vulnerabilities in ./src

 do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

 The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N> . The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

 Requirements

- A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents

- Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators

- An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

 Design principles

- Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.

- Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.

- Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.

- Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.

- Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

 Contact

 Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

 Your coding agent forgets everything between sessions. Claude-Mem remembers for it.

 Quick Start •
 How It Works •
 Search Tools •
 Documentation •
 Configuration •
 Troubleshooting •
 License

 Every new session, your agent starts from zero. It re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and walks back into mistakes you already fixed together.

 Claude-Mem runs a second agent beside it that takes notes while it works. The next session starts with a short index of what matters, and pulls in the details only when it needs them. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 11 more agents. Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp can search your memory, but their sessions aren't recorded.

 Quick Start

 Installing for someone as an AI agent? Run npx claude-mem install --runtime worker on their computer in an interactive terminal (enable PTY in your shell tool). It first asks in the terminal which agents to set up and, for Claude Code, whether to disable native auto-memory (and whether to overwrite an existing install). Relay each question to the user and type their answer, or pass --ide <id> to skip the first one. Keep the installer running. When it prints Continue setup in your browser , open that URL in the user's browser if the installer hasn't already opened it. Let the user go through setup and make their own choices, including the usage-analytics question the installer may ask at the end. If you can't run an interactive terminal on their computer, give them the command to run locally.

 npx claude-mem install

 The installer finds the agents on your machine and asks which ones to set up. Then just start working: observations stream in from your first prompt, and your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. (Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp get memory search only, so their sessions don't add to it.)

 The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link, no card required to sign in). Choosing the claude-mem observer then starts its 30 Day Free Trial on a checkout page that asks for a payment method; once it completes, the installer saves your memory key. With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider: the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.

 Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit --provider flag, set CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false , or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.

 Your memory lives in ~/.claude-mem on your machine. Cloud sync is opt-in. Anonymous usage analytics are on by default; npx claude-mem telemetry disable turns them off ( what's collected ).

 Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code:

 /plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem

/plugin install claude-mem

 Restart Claude Code. Context from previous sessions will automatically appear in new sessions.

 Note: Claude-Mem is also published on npm, but npm install -g claude-mem installs the SDK/library only — it does not register the plugin hooks or set up the worker service. Always install via npx claude-mem install or the /plugin commands above.

 Other agents

 npx claude-mem install covers every supported agent. To set up one agent directly, pass --ide .

 OpenCode (1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2). Restart OpenCode after installing.

 npx claude-mem install --ide opencode

 T3 Code (Codex and Claude Code providers). The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the T3 Code integration guide for custom server settings, status, and removal.

 npx claude-mem install --ide t3code

 Antigravity CLI ( setup guide ):

 npx claude-mem install --ide antigravity

 OMP (Oh My Pi):

 npx claude-mem install --ide omp

 Pi and DeepSeek Harness use the worker runtime. See native harness setup for capture, recall, and troubleshooting.

 npx claude-mem install --ide pi
npx claude-mem install --ide dsh --dsh-profile tui

 Grok Bot: see Grok Bot below.

 npx claude-mem install --ide grok-bot

 The full list of --ide values is in npx claude-mem --help .

 Grok Bot

 Grok Bot has no host hooks, so we watch the chat log files. Default is CMEM Pro, the hosted memory. Local observer is opt-in: --provider host . Installing this plugin does not install Cursor.

 Opt-in awareness push: needle observations ( decision , bugfix , security_alert , sensitive ) are appended as dated - YYYY-MM-DD [awareness] … lines into that bot's memory/log/YYYY-MM.md . Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write profile.md , user-memory, or project memory. Enable with CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=true and set CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_AGENT_IDS to your agent UUIDs (empty by default).

 🦞 OpenClaw Gateway

 Install claude-mem as a persistent memory plugin on OpenClaw gateways with a single command:

 curl -fsSL https://install.cmem.ai/openclaw.sh | bash

 The installer handles dependencies, plugin setup, AI provider configuration, worker startup, and optional real-time observation feeds to Telegram, Discord, Slack, and more. See the OpenClaw Integration Guide for details.

 What You Get

- 🧠 The next session starts where the last one left off. Each session opens with a compact index of past observations, layered so the agent opens full details only when it needs them, and the header can show what each layer costs in tokens.

- 🔍 Find anything you worked on. The mem-search skill searches your project history in three steps (index, timeline, details), so the agent spends tokens only on what it opens.

- 🖥️ Watch it work, and keep track of yours. My Work shows live requests, progress, human handoffs and a saved review queue at the worker URL printed on startup. Guide . Memory, sessions and settings remain at /viewer .

- 👥 Share with your team, if you want. TeamBrain is an optional shared workspace beside My Work, with real team work lists, member attribution and linked findings. Each person chooses what to share; personal requests and review notes stay separate. Set up a team .

- 💻 Search from Claude Desktop. Search your memory from Claude Desktop conversations.

- 🔒 Keep secrets out. Wrap anything in <private> tags and it never gets stored.

- 🖼️ Screenshots, kept by default. Keep converted copies of tool screenshots under ~/.claude-mem/media-v1/ and show them in My Work, upload them to cmem.ai only when Cloud Sync is on, and send them to the observer model only when image inference is separately enabled. Turn it off with the "Keep images" switch in Settings ( details ).

- ⚙️ Choose what gets injected. Fine-grained settings for what context a new session starts with.

- 🤖 Nothing to remember to do. It runs on its own once installed.

- 🔗 Point back to past work. Every observation has an ID you can cite through the worker API or open in the web viewer.

 Documentation

 📚 View Full Documentation - Browse on official website

 Getting Started

- Installation Guide - Quick start & advanced installation

- Usage Guide - How Claude-Mem works automatically

- Search Tools - Query your project history with natural language

- Cloud Sync - Back up your memory to cmem.ai — no daemon, the worker syncs on write

 Best Practices

- Context Engineering - AI agent context optimization principles

- Progressive Disclosure - Philosophy behind Claude-Mem's context priming strategy

 Architecture

- Overview - System components & data flow

- Architecture Evolution - The journey from v3 to v5

- Hooks Architecture - How Claude-Mem uses lifecycle hooks

- Hooks Reference - Every hook entry explained

- Worker Service - HTTP API & Bun management

- Database - SQLite schema & FTS5 search

- Search Architecture - Hybrid search with Chroma vector database

 Configuration & Development

- Configuration - Environment variables & settings

- Development - Building, testing, contributing

- Troubleshooting - Common issues & solutions

 How It Works

- Your agent works. Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker.

- The observer takes notes. A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends.

- The next session starts with them. When a session starts, your agent gets a compact index of the observations that matter for this project, and fetches full details only when it needs them.

 Memory injection starts on your second session in a project. To front-load a whole repo instead, run /learn-codebase (~5 minutes on a typical repo, optional).

 See Architecture Overview for details.

 How it fits together

 For contributors, the main parts and where they live:

- The claude-mem command ( src/npx-cli/index.ts ): install, repair, doctor, start, search and the rest. The installer puts a small launcher on PATH so hooks can run claude-mem directly.

- Hooks ( src/cli/hook-command.ts , one adapter per agent in src/cli/adapters/ ): each agent event runs one shell-free command, such as claude-mem hook claude-code <event> . For Claude Code that's Setup ( claude --init / --maintenance ), SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SubagentStop and SessionEnd.

- The worker ( src/services/worker-service.ts , routes in src/services/worker/http/routes/ ): a local HTTP service managed by Bun. It takes tool activity from the hooks, runs the observer, and serves the viewer and search.

- The observer (prompts in src/sdk/ , one provider per model source in src/services/worker/ , such as ClaudeProvider.ts and OpenRouterProvider.ts ): turns tool activity into observations and summaries.

- Storage ( src/services/sqlite/ ): SQLite at ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db holds sessions, observations and summaries. Chroma adds semantic search on top of SQLite's keyword search ( src/services/worker/search/ ).

- Context ( src/services/context/ ): builds the block a new session starts with.

- Search ( src/servers/mcp-server.ts , plugin/skills/mem-search/ ): the MCP tools and the mem-search skill that drives them.

- The viewer ( src/ui/viewer/ at /viewer , src/ui/my-work/ at / ): memory, sessions and settings, plus My Work.

- The built plugin ( plugin/ ): written by npm run build ; edit src/ , not the generated scripts.

 The words we use for each of these, and the story they tell, are in docs/story.md .

 MCP Search Tools

 Search runs through three MCP tools in a token-efficient three-step workflow. The mem-search skill drives it for you:

 The three steps:

- search - Get compact index with IDs (~50-100 tokens/result)

- timeline - Get chronological context around interesting results

- get_observations - Fetch full details ONLY for filtered IDs (~500-1,000 tokens/result)

 Step by step:

- Your agent uses MCP tools to search your memory

- Start with search to get an index of results

- Use timeline to see what was happening around specific observations

- Use get_observations to fetch full details for relevant IDs

- ~10x token savings by filtering before fetching details

representativeRepos.readmeText:
T3 Code

 T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

 Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

 "Wait, what are you selling me?"

 Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

 We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

 Installation

 Warning
 T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

- Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

- Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

- Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

- Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

- OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

- Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

- fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

 Command line

 curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

 On Windows, in PowerShell:

 irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

 Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

 To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

 Desktop app

 Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

 Windows ( winget )

 winget install T3Tools.T3Code

representativeRepos.readmeText:
agent-desktop

 Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

 agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

 Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.

 Install

 npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant

 Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
 GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

 On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop . There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.

 Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation .

 Quick start

 agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify

 Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:

 {
 "version" : " 2.6 " ,
 "ok" : true ,
 "command" : " snapshot " ,
 "data" : {
 "app" : " Finder " ,
 "snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " ,
 "ref_count" : 59 ,
 "complete" : true ,
 "tree" : {
 "role" : " window " ,
 "name" : " Downloads " ,
 "children" : [
 { "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] }
 ]
 }
 }
}

- Refs belong to their snapshot. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action
returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET : take a new snapshot and use its refs.

- Several windows give AMBIGUOUS_TARGET ; snapshot lists the candidate window ids in error.details . Pass one
with --window-id .

- Dense apps: map first with snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact , then drill into one region with
 snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact .

- Headless by default. Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global
 --headed flag allows physical input.

- Post-action waits observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window,
including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep
their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay
selectors share its scope. Wait scope and results
describe the selector limits.

- type , set-value , and clipboard-set accept --stdin for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments.

- PowerShell. Quote every ref ( '@s8f3k2p9:e8' ), because a bare @token is the splatting operator.

 The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

 How it works

 Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter . Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.

 For AI agents

 The binary carries guides that match its version:

 agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop < command > --help # flags for one command

 Install the skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

 Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

 Use ` agent-desktop ` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
 ` agent-desktop skills get desktop ` and ` agent-desktop skills get platform ` , and follow them.

 Retry a failed command only when error.disposition.retry is safe . See JSON output for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.

 MCP

 agent-desktop mcp serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command ( desktop_snapshot , desktop_click , desktop_session_start ), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:

 { "mcpServers" : { "agent-desktop" : { "command" : " agent-desktop " , "args" : [ " mcp " ] } } }

 Global flags given to mcp , such as --session , --headed or --trace , apply to every call.

 Commands

 agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four ( key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up ) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. Commands documents each one.

 Group
 Commands

 Observe
 snapshot , find , get , is , screenshot , list-surfaces

 Act on a ref
 click , double-click , triple-click , right-click , type , set-value , clear , focus , select , toggle , check , uncheck , expand , collapse , scroll , scroll-to

 Keyboard and mouse
 press , hover , drag , mouse-move , mouse-click , mouse-wheel , key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up

 Apps and windows
 launch , close-app , list-apps , list-windows , list-displays , focus-window , resize-window , move-window , minimize , maximize , restore , open-system-surface

 Notifications
 list-notifications , dismiss-notification , dismiss-all-notifications , notification-action

 Clipboard
 clipboard-get , clipboard-set , clipboard-clear

 Wait
 wait

 Sessions
 session , trace , cursor-overlay

 System
 status , permissions , version , batch , skills

 Platform support

 Platform
 Requirement
 Accessibility API

 macOS
 macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple Silicon
 AX API

 Windows
 Windows 10 1809 or later, x64 or ARM64
 UI Automation

 Linux
 Ubuntu 24.04 or later, x86_64 or aarch64, X11 or Wayland
 AT-SPI

 Each platform page lists what works headless, what needs --headed , and what refuses.

 C library

 Each release ships libagent_desktop_ffi , so a program can call agent-desktop in process. See the C library docs .

 import ctypes
 lib = ctypes . CDLL ( "./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib" )
 lib . ad_adapter_create . restype = ctypes . c_void_p
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy . argtypes = [ ctypes . c_void_p ]
 assert lib . ad_init ( 7 ) == 0 # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library
 adapter = lib . ad_adapter_create ()
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy ( adapter )

 Development

 Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS:

 HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi)
cargo test " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} "
cargo clippy " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} " --all-targets -- -D warnings

 On Windows, use agent-desktop-windows instead of agent-desktop-macos ; on Linux, agent-desktop-linux . CONTRIBUTING.md lists every gate.

 Documentation

- Introduction : what it is and how it works

- Snapshots and refs

- Errors and recovery

- Skills

- CONCEPTS.md : vocabulary

- CONTRIBUTING.md , SECURITY.md , SUPPORT.md

representativeRepos.readmeText:
security-audit

 A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

 This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness . The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

 What it does

 The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

- Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json .

- Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.

- Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.

- Structured output -- write confirmed , needs_validation , and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json .

- Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.

- Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md , FINDINGS-DETAIL.md , and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

 The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

 The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

 Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

 Files

 File
 Purpose

 SKILL.md
 Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns

 RECONNAISSANCE.md
 Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions

 HUNTING.md
 Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules

 ATTACK-CLASSES.md
 Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts

 MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md
 Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets

 AI-AND-LLM.md
 Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets

 WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md
 HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets

 CLIENT-SIDE.md
 DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets

 SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md
 Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes

 CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md
 IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes

 PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md
 RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes

 RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md
 Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes

 DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md
 Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes

 DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md
 Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes

 VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md
 Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting

 report-schema.json
 JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts

 validate-findings.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5

 validate-findings.test.cjs
 Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks

 validate-coverage-ledger.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5

 validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs
 Coverage-ledger validator tests

 Installation

 Install the skill with the Skills CLI :

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit

 Use --global for a user-level installation:

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit \
 --global

 Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

 Usage

 Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

 security audit this codebase

 find security vulnerabilities in ./src

 do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

 The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N> . The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

 Requirements

- A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents

- Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators

- An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

 Design principles

- Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.

- Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.

- Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.

- Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.

- Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

 Contact

 Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

 License

 MIT -- see LICENSE .

readmeText:
Claude Code Game Studios

 Describe a game. Claude Code asks a few questions, writes a one-page brief,
 and builds a playable browser game from it.

 Then you change it, grow it and finish it, one step at a time.

 Make me a game

 Open Claude Code in a copy of this repository and say what you want:

 /prototype a fishing game where the rare fish only bite at dusk

- A few questions. One round, picked from the genre: the choices that
shape the game, how it should feel, how it looks, how hard it is, the goal.
Each has a usual answer, so "you pick" works. A vague idea ("a racing game")
gets two or three one-line pitches to choose from first.

- A one-page brief. design/game-brief.md : your words kept as you typed
them, the look, the first minute, the challenge, the features and what is
left for later. You read it and say Build it, or change something first.

- A first build. A browser game in prototypes/<name>/ that opens with a
double-click: every figure drawn, no emoji art, no copy of another game, and
not trivially easy. Your session builds it at its own effort ("build it at
medium" is cheaper and thinner).

- Checked before you get it. A few scripted key presses in a headless
browser show it opens with no errors and responds; text that is too small,
overlapping or off screen and screens that freeze are fixed in one round; and
every line of the brief is marked built, missing or broken from the
screenshots and the code, or not assessed when it could not be checked. Your
play is the real test: the handover card says what passed, what is still broken
and what was guessed, and ends "Not yet played by a person".

 Then it is yours to play. After that:

- Change it by asking. Each change is checked against what you said to
keep and to avoid, and each one you accept is a checkpoint you can go back
to. Ask to tune it and it gains a tweak panel with a slider for every value.

- Share it. A clean copy without the panel and the working files, ready
for itch.io or a link.

- Grow it. When you like it, it becomes a real web project (Vite and
TypeScript, its values in data files, tests and a build), and you add to it
one feature a sitting: say the next feature, and it is built, checked and
committed. After every feature the same seeded run is played again and any
change is shown to you. Stories ( /create-stories , /dev-story ,
 /story-done ) only when you ask for them.

- Finish it. /cut proposes what to cut and a polish list, and a date
when the game is to sell.

 Already have a browser game? /prototype --from <path> brings a copy in as it
is, so it can be changed and grown the same way.

 What it has been shown to do

- The first build. In a blind comparison on three game ideas, the brief
made from its questions was picked over a hand-written brief all three
times. All six games built from the two kinds of brief were ones the tester
said they would build on, so on the games themselves the two kinds of brief
tied.

- Growing. One game was grown from its first build through six stories
into a game the tester would keep building. That is one game, not yet a
pattern.

- Not yet shown: the engine route (Godot, Unity, Unreal) and deepening one
system with a design document. Both are built and pass the framework's own
checks, but neither has had a test like the two above.

 The games themselves are deliberately not shipped here: this is a template
you clone to start your own project, and somebody else's game in your repo is
clutter, not evidence.

 Table of Contents

- Getting Started

- Engines

- Configuration

- Upgrading

- Project Structure

- Hooks, Permissions and Rules

- Studio Mode

- Design Philosophy

- Customization

- Platform Support

- Community

- Supporting This Project

- License

 Getting Started

 Prerequisites

- Git

- Claude Code — the native installer is recommended ( npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code also works, on Node.js 22+)

- Python 3 — reads project.yaml for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default

- Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with Git for Windows . Without it on Windows the hooks skip themselves, and session start says their checks are off

- Chrome, Edge or Chromium — /prototype plays and screenshots each game in it; without one, those checks say they were not assessed

- Recommended : Node.js (to grow a game into a web project, for a 3D game's three.js, and for the web engine's build and tests) and jq (for hook validation)

 Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it.

 Setup

-
 Clone or use as template :

 git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game
 cd my-game

-
 Open Claude Code in the project's root folder (the one holding
 CLAUDE.md and project.yaml ) and start a session:

 claude

 Starting it in a subfolder such as src/ skips the project's hooks, deny
rules and ask-first permission mode.

-
 Type /prototype and your idea , or run /start , which asks where
you are (make me a game, an idea or none yet, clear design, existing work)
and guides you to the right workflow. No assumptions.

 Other ways in:

- /next-step — names the one next step wherever you are

- /brainstorm — explore game ideas from scratch

- /setup-engine godot 4.7 — configure an engine if you already know you want one

- /project-stage-detect — analyze an existing project

 Engines

 Engine
 engine.name
 Code root
 Notes

 Web
 Web
 src/
 The default for a new project. A one-shot needs no engine at all; a grown game is a web project. /setup-engine web offers a starter: nothing extra, three.js, Phaser or PixiJS

 Godot 4
 Godot
 src/
 GDScript, C# or GDExtension

 Unity
 Unity
 Assets/
 Unity compiles only Assets/ and Packages/

 Unreal Engine 5
 Unreal
 Source/<Module>/
 C++ and Blueprints

 /setup-engine pins the engine version and writes its reference docs
( docs/engine-reference/<engine>/ ). With no engine set, /prototype builds
in the browser first; you pick an engine after you have played the game. Each
engine's folders and default commands come from one table,
 .claude/engines/engines.tsv . If your code or tests live somewhere else, set
 engine.code_root or engine.test_root in project.yaml .

 Configuration

 project.yaml at the repo root is the single source of truth for how the
studio behaves on your project — engine, naming conventions, and a modes
block that controls how much process every skill enforces. /start writes it
for you; you rarely need to hand-edit it.

 The one question that matters most is modes.rigor — minimal , standard ,
or full . It's a single front door over six separate knobs ( workflow —
which GDD sections are required, docs.density , qa.level ,
 story_granularity , review_mode — how many director agents review your work,
and team.size ), so /start asks it once instead of six times:

- minimal (default) — the light path. No GDDs required, terse docs, minimal QA evidence, solo review. /prototype (questions, a brief, a first build) → play and change it → grow it on PROCEED → one feature a sitting: name it, and it is built, checked and committed. Stories ( /create-stories → /dev-story ↔ /story-done ) only when you ask.

- standard — 5 required GDD sections, balanced doc depth, standard QA evidence, lean review.

- full — all 8 GDD sections, thorough docs, full QA evidence on every story type, full director review.

 minimal is the default because the heavier tier costs more to reach working
code without producing a better result, and gives nothing back when someone new
picks the project up. Raise it in one /project-settings call when your project grows
— /next-step and /gate-check will suggest it when they see the signs.

 Two escape hatches keep one setting from being a blunt instrument.
 system_overrides holds a single system to a higher standard than the rest
of the project — your combat system gets the full treatment while everything
else stays light. testing.strict sets, per test type (logic, integration,
visual, UI, config), whether missing evidence blocks a story or merely warns.

 Any of the six underlying knobs can still be set individually if you want a mix
(e.g. workflow: full with docs.density: terse — comprehensive but compact).
Two of them — review_mode ( full / lean / solo ) and team.size — are
also personal : rigor sets the team-wide default, but you can override them
per-developer in a gitignored project.local.yaml without touching the shared
config. modes.automation (how often the AI pauses to ask before it acts) sits
outside rigor and is likewise personally overridable. project.goal (a jam
game, a hobby, a game to sell, and so on) is what you want from the game;
 /start guesses it, and /cut reads it.

 View or change any setting with the /project-settings skill:

 /project-settings # view effective config
/project-settings modes.review_mode # view one setting
/project-settings modes.rigor=full # write to project.yaml (team-wide)
/project-settings --local modes.review_mode=solo # write to project.local.yaml (just you)

 Full schema and per-setting behavior: .claude/docs/effects-map.md .

 Upgrading

 Already using an older version of this template? See UPGRADING.md
for step-by-step migration instructions, a breakdown of what changed between
versions, and which files are safe to overwrite vs. which need a manual merge.

 Project Structure

 CLAUDE.md # Master configuration
project.yaml # Project settings: engine, modes, goal
.claude/
 settings.json # Hooks, permissions, safety rules
 agents/ # 49 agent definitions (markdown + YAML frontmatter)
 skills/ # 75 skills, plus three old names (a subdirectory each)
 hooks/ # 18 scripts (bash) — 15 event hooks, two helpers they
 # source (yaml-helper.sh, update-check.sh), and one
 # opt-in diagnostic you wire yourself
 scripts/ # Helper scripts the skills and hooks run; each .sh has --help
 rules/ # 14 path-scoped coding standards
 genres/ # Genre sheets and look guidance /prototype asks and
 # builds from
 engines/ # The engine table (engines.tsv) and the web starter
 statusline.sh # Status line script (context%, model, stage, epic breadcrumb)
 docs/
 workflow-catalog.yaml # 7-phase pipeline definition (read by /next-step)
 templates/ # 62 document templates (+ per-section guidance)
prototypes/ # One-shots, one folder each (isolated from src/)
references/ # Optional: images and sounds you like, for /prototype
src/ # Game source code (Godot, Web). The code root is
 # ENGINE-SPECIFIC: Unity compiles only
 # Assets/, Unreal builds from Source/<Module>/
assets/ # Art, audio, VFX, shaders, data files
design/ # The game brief, GDDs, narrative docs, level designs
docs/ # Technical documentation, ADRs, engine references
tests/ # Test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest)
tools/ # Build and pipeline tools
production/ # Sprint plans, milestones, release tracking
studio-tests/ # QA for the skills and agents themselves — see below

 Testing your customizations

 Claude Code Game Studios is a template you are meant to edit. studio-tests/ is how
you check that an edited or newly written skill still holds up — a catalog of all
75 skills and 49 agents, per-category quality rubrics, behavioral specs, and
templates for writing specs of your own.

 /skill-test static [name] # structural linter — 7 compliance checks
/skill-test category [name] # category-specific quality rubric
/skill-test spec [name] # behavioral spec assertions
/skill-test audit # coverage report across skills and agents
/skill-improve [name] # test-fix-retest loop; keeps or reverts on score change

 It tests the framework , never your game — game tests live in tests/ .

 Hooks, Permissions and Rules

 Hooks run automatically on every session:

 Trigger
 What It Does

 PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell)
 Checks for hardcoded values, TO...

representativeRepos.readmeText:
T3 Code

 T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

 Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

 "Wait, what are you selling me?"

 Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

 We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

 Installation

 Warning
 T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

- Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

- Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

- Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

- Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

- OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

- Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

- fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

 Command line

 curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

 On Windows, in PowerShell:

 irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

 Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

 To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

 Desktop app

 Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

 Windows ( winget )

 winget install T3Tools.T3Code

 Windows ( scoop )

 scoop install extras/t3code

 macOS (Homebrew)

 brew install --cask t3-code

 Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

 Download the .deb from GitHub Releases , then:

 sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

 Arch Linux (AUR)

 Stable:

 yay -S t3code-bin

 Nightly:

 yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

 The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

 Nix (nixpkgs)

 nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

 The package is maintained in nixpkgs
and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.
See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

 Some notes

 We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

 We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

 Documentation

 Full docs live in docs/ . There's no docs site yet.

- FAQ

- Install and first run

- Permission modes

- Keyboard shortcuts

- Project settings

- Appearance preferences

- Remote access from a phone or another machine

- Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP

- Keeping app and server in sync

- Source control integrations

- Multiple accounts: Codex · Claude

- Run T3 Code as a background service

 Building from source? Start at docs/internals/overview.md .

 If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

 Install vp

 T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global vp command-line tool.

 macOS / Linux

 curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

 Windows

 irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

 Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

 Install dependencies

 vp i

 Read CONTRIBUTING.md before reporting a bug or opening a PR.

 Have a feature request? Start an Ideas discussion .

 Need support? Join the Discord .

representativeRepos.readmeText:
agent-desktop

 Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

 agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

 Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.

 Install

 npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant

 Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
 GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

 On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop . There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.

 Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation .

 Quick start

 agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify

 Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:

 {
 "version" : " 2.6 " ,
 "ok" : true ,
 "command" : " snapshot " ,
 "data" : {
 "app" : " Finder " ,
 "snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " ,
 "ref_count" : 59 ,
 "complete" : true ,
 "tree" : {
 "role" : " window " ,
 "name" : " Downloads " ,
 "children" : [
 { "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] }
 ]
 }
 }
}

- Refs belong to their snapshot. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action
returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET : take a new snapshot and use its refs.

- Several windows give AMBIGUOUS_TARGET ; snapshot lists the candidate window ids in error.details . Pass one
with --window-id .

- Dense apps: map first with snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact , then drill into one region with
 snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact .

- Headless by default. Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global
 --headed flag allows physical input.

- Post-action waits observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window,
including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep
their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay
selectors share its scope. Wait scope and results
describe the selector limits.

- type , set-value , and clipboard-set accept --stdin for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments.

- PowerShell. Quote every ref ( '@s8f3k2p9:e8' ), because a bare @token is the splatting operator.

 The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

 How it works

 Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter . Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.

 For AI agents

 The binary carries guides that match its version:

 agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop < command > --help # flags for one command

 Install the skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

 Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

 Use ` agent-desktop ` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
 ` agent-desktop skills get desktop ` and ` agent-desktop skills get platform ` , and follow them.

 Retry a failed command only when error.disposition.retry is safe . See JSON output for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.

 MCP

 agent-desktop mcp serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command ( desktop_snapshot , desktop_click , desktop_session_start ), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:

 { "mcpServers" : { "agent-desktop" : { "command" : " agent-desktop " , "args" : [ " mcp " ] } } }

 Global flags given to mcp , such as --session , --headed or --trace , apply to every call.

 Commands

 agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four ( key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up ) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. Commands documents each one.

 Group
 Commands

 Observe

 Act on a ref

 Keyboard and mouse
 press , hover , drag , mouse-move , mouse-click , mouse-wheel , key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up

 Apps and windows
 launch , close-app , list-apps , list-windows , list-displays , focus-window , resize-window , move-window , minimize , maximize , restore , open-system-surface

 Notifications
 list-notifications , dismiss-notification , dismiss-all-notifications , notification-action

 Clipboard
 clipboard-get , clipboard-set , clipboard-clear

 Wait

 System

 Platform support

 Each platform page lists what works headless, what needs --headed , and what refuses.

 C library

 Each release ships libagent_desktop_ffi , so a program can call agent-desktop in process. See the C library docs .

 import ctypes
 lib = ctypes . CDLL ( "./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib" )
 lib . ad_adapter_create . restype = ctypes . c_void_p
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy . argtypes = [ ctypes . c_void_p ]
 assert lib . ad_init ( 7 ) == 0 # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library
 adapter = lib . ad_adapter_create ()
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy ( adapter )

 Development

 Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS:

 HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi)
cargo test " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} "
cargo clippy " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} " --all-targets -- -D warnings

 On Windows, use agent-desktop-windows instead of agent-desktop-macos ; on Linux, agent-desktop-linux . CONTRIBUTING.md lists every gate.

representativeRepos.readmeText:
security-audit

 A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

 This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness . The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

 What it does

 The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

- Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json .

- Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.

- Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.

- Structured output -- write confirmed , needs_validation , and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json .

- Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.

- Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md , FINDINGS-DETAIL.md , and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

 The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

 The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

 Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

 Files

 File
 Purpose

 SKILL.md
 Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns

 RECONNAISSANCE.md
 Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions

 HUNTING.md
 Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules

 ATTACK-CLASSES.md
 Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts

 MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md
 Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets

 AI-AND-LLM.md
 Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets

 WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md
 HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets

 CLIENT-SIDE.md
 DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets

 SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md
 Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes

 CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md
 IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes

 PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md
 RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes

 RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md
 Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes

 DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md
 Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes

 DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md
 Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes

 VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md
 Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting

 report-schema.json
 JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts

 validate-findings.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5

 validate-findings.test.cjs
 Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks

 validate-coverage-ledger.cjs
 Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5

 validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs
 Coverage-ledger validator tests

 Installation

 Install the skill with the Skills CLI :

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit

 Use --global for a user-level installation:

 npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
 --skill security-audit \
 --global

 Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

 Usage

 Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

 security audit this codebase

 find security vulnerabilities in ./src

 do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

 The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N> . The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

 Requirements

- A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents

- Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators

- An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

 Design principles

- Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.

- Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.

- Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.

- Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.

- Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

 Contact

 Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

 License

 MIT -- see LICENSE .

readmeText:
agent-browser

 Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

 agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

 Install

 npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only)

- Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install .

- Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries.

- No install: npx agent-browser open example.com .

 Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation .

 Quick start

 agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-browser get url # check the result
agent-browser close

 The snapshot for example.com :

 - link "Learn more" [ref=e1]

- Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again.

- CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors .

- A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry.

 The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

 How it works

 The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured.

 Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect ( CDP mode ), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine , drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator , or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase , Browserless , Browser Use , Kernel , or AgentCore .

 For AI agents

 The CLI ships skills that match its version:

 agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows
agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list
agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates
agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more

 Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

 npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser

 The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core , so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

 Use ` agent-browser ` for browser automation. Before the first use, run
 ` agent-browser skills get core ` and follow it.

 For MCP clients, agent-browser mcp starts an MCP server over stdio. See MCP server .

 Commands

 Run agent-browser --help for the full list, or agent-browser <command> --help for one command.

 Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host.

 Development

 Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust:

 Run the Rust checks from cli/ :

cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1 # launches real headless Chrome

representativeRepos.readmeText:
T3 Code

 T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

 Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

 "Wait, what are you selling me?"

 Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

 We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

 Installation

 Warning
 T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

- Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

- Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

- Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

- Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

- OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

- Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

- fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

 Command line

 curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

 On Windows, in PowerShell:

 irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

 Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

 To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

 Desktop app

 Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

 Windows ( winget )

 winget install T3Tools.T3Code

 Windows ( scoop )

 scoop install extras/t3code

 macOS (Homebrew)

 brew install --cask t3-code

 Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

 Download the .deb from GitHub Releases , then:

 sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

 Arch Linux (AUR)

 Stable:

 yay -S t3code-bin

 Nightly:

 yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

 The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

 Nix (nixpkgs)

 nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

 The package is maintained in nixpkgs
and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.
See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

 Some notes

 We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

 We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

 Documentation

 Full docs live in docs/ . There's no docs site yet.

- FAQ

- Install and first run

- Permission modes

- Keyboard shortcuts

- Project settings

- Appearance preferences

- Remote access from a phone or another machine

- Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP

- Keeping app and server in sync

- Source control integrations

- Multiple accounts: Codex · Claude

- Run T3 Code as a background service

 Building from source? Start at docs/internals/overview.md .

 If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

 Install vp

 T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global vp command-line tool.

 macOS / Linux

 curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

 Windows

 irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

 Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

 Install dependencies

 vp i

 Read CONTRIBUTING.md before reporting a bug or opening a PR.

 Have a feature request? Start an Ideas discussion .

 Need support? Join the Discord .

representativeRepos.readmeText:
agent-desktop

 Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

 agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

 Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.

 Install

 npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant

 Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
 GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

 On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop . There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.

 Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation .

 Quick start

 agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify

 Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:

 {
 "version" : " 2.6 " ,
 "ok" : true ,
 "command" : " snapshot " ,
 "data" : {
 "app" : " Finder " ,
 "snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " ,
 "ref_count" : 59 ,
 "complete" : true ,
 "tree" : {
 "role" : " window " ,
 "name" : " Downloads " ,
 "children" : [
 { "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] }
 ]
 }
 }
}

- Refs belong to their snapshot. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action
returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET : take a new snapshot and use its refs.

- Several windows give AMBIGUOUS_TARGET ; snapshot lists the candidate window ids in error.details . Pass one
with --window-id .

- Dense apps: map first with snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact , then drill into one region with
 snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact .

- Headless by default. Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global
 --headed flag allows physical input.

- Post-action waits observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window,
including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep
their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay
selectors share its scope. Wait scope and results
describe the selector limits.

- type , set-value , and clipboard-set accept --stdin for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments.

- PowerShell. Quote every ref ( '@s8f3k2p9:e8' ), because a bare @token is the splatting operator.

 The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

 How it works

 Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter . Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.

 For AI agents

 The binary carries guides that match its version:

 agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop < command > --help # flags for one command

 Install the skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

 Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

 Use ` agent-desktop ` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
 ` agent-desktop skills get desktop ` and ` agent-desktop skills get platform ` , and follow them.

 Retry a failed command only when error.disposition.retry is safe . See JSON output for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.

 MCP

 agent-desktop mcp serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command ( desktop_snapshot , desktop_click , desktop_session_start ), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:

 { "mcpServers" : { "agent-desktop" : { "command" : " agent-desktop " , "args" : [ " mcp " ] } } }

 Global flags given to mcp , such as --session , --headed or --trace , apply to every call.

 Commands

 agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four ( key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up ) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. Commands documents each one.

 Group
 Commands

 Observe
 snapshot , find , get , is , screenshot , list-surfaces

 Act on a ref
 click , double-click , triple-click , right-click , type , set-value , clear , focus , select , toggle , check , uncheck , expand , collapse , scroll , scroll-to

 Keyboard and mouse
 press , hover , drag , mouse-move , mouse-click , mouse-wheel , key-down , key-up , mouse-down , mouse-up

 Apps and windows
 launch , close-app , list-apps , list-windows , list-displays , focus-window , resize-window , move-window , minimize , maximize , restore , open-system-surface

 Notifications
 list-notifications , dismiss-notification , dismiss-all-notifications , notification-action

 Clipboard
 clipboard-get , clipboard-set , clipboard-clear

 Wait
 wait

 Sessions
 session , trace , cursor-overlay

 System
 status , permissions , version , batch , skills

 Platform support

 Platform
 Requirement
 Accessibility API

 macOS
 macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple Silicon
 AX API

 Windows
 Windows 10 1809 or later, x64 or ARM64
 UI Automation

 Linux
 Ubuntu 24.04 or later, x86_64 or aarch64, X11 or Wayland
 AT-SPI

 Each platform page lists what works headless, what needs --headed , and what refuses.

 C library

 Each release ships libagent_desktop_ffi , so a program can call agent-desktop in process. See the C library docs .

 import ctypes
 lib = ctypes . CDLL ( "./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib" )
 lib . ad_adapter_create . restype = ctypes . c_void_p
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy . argtypes = [ ctypes . c_void_p ]
 assert lib . ad_init ( 7 ) == 0 # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library
 adapter = lib . ad_adapter_create ()
 lib . ad_adapter_destroy ( adapter )

 Development

 Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS:

 HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi)
cargo test " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} "
cargo clippy " ${HOST_PKGS[@]} " --all-targets -- -D warnings

 On Windows, use agent-desktop-windows instead of agent-desktop-macos ; on Linux, agent-desktop-linux . CONTRIBUTING.md lists every gate.

 Documentation

- Introduction : what it is and how it works

- Snapshots and refs

- Errors and recovery

- Skills

- CONCEPTS.md : vocabulary

- CONTRIBUTING.md , SECURITY.md , SUPPORT.md

 License

 Apache-2.0
